title: What is a skills taxonomy?
description: A skills taxonomy is a structured, shared vocabulary that names, defines and groups skills. What it contains, public examples, and how it differs.
shortAnswer: A skills taxonomy is a structured vocabulary that names, defines and groups skills into categories, usually as a hierarchy from broad skill families down to specific skills. It gives employers, educators and governments one shared language for describing what people can do, so job requirements, training content, assessment results and workforce data can be compared and combined. It describes skills; it does not by itself set the standard for competent performance in a role.
keyTakeaways: A skills taxonomy organizes skills into categories or clusters based on their definitions; its structure and level of detail depend on what it will be used for.

Public taxonomies such as the European Commission's ESCO classification, the SFIA framework for digital skills, and national taxonomies in development, such as Australia's National Skills Taxonomy, are common reference points.
Useful taxonomies are dynamic, comprehensive, interoperable, accessible, customizable and granular enough for their purpose.
A taxonomy supplies names and definitions; a competency framework adds performance standards and evidence; a skills matrix records who holds which skills.

sections.heading: What does a skills taxonomy contain?

blocks.text: A skills taxonomy contains a list of skills, a definition for each, and a grouping structure that places each skill in a family or cluster. Larger taxonomies add metadata such as alternative labels, skill type, how widely a skill applies across occupations, and links to occupations or qualifications.

The World Economic Forum's [Global Skills Taxonomy Adoption Toolkit](https://www3.weforum.org/docs/WEF_Global_Skills_Taxonomy_Adoption_Toolkit_2025.pdf) (January 2025) gives a short working definition: "A skills taxonomy organizes skills into categories or clusters based on their definitions. Both the structure and detail of a taxonomy vary depending on its intended use." The same glossary separates skills, "the capabilities needed to complete a task", from knowledge, "the body of facts, principles and theories that are related to a field of work or study".

The European Commission's [ESCO skills pillar](https://esco.ec.europa.eu/en/classification/skill) shows what a mature taxonomy looks like. ESCO v1.2.1 lists 13,939 skill and knowledge concepts in four sub-classifications (knowledge, language skills and knowledge, skills, and transversal skills). Each concept has a preferred term, alternative terms in 28 languages, a description, a reusability level (transversal, cross-sectoral, sector-specific or occupation-specific) and relationships to other skills and occupations. ESCO states that there is "no distinction between skills and competences".

sections.heading: Which public skills taxonomies are used as reference points?

blocks.text: The most common reference points are regional and national classifications published by governments, plus sector frameworks maintained by independent bodies. Organizations rarely build a taxonomy from nothing; they adopt one of these and adapt it.

blocks.text: Jobs and Skills Australia describes its [National Skills Taxonomy](https://www.jobsandskills.gov.au/data/national-skills-taxonomy) as "a new, evidence-based framework that provides a common language for describing the skills Australians gain, develop, and use across education and employment", designed to be interoperable with existing education and occupation frameworks. Japan's [Digital Skill Standard](https://www.ipa.go.jp/jinzai/skill-standard/dss/index.html), published by IPA with METI, is an example of a taxonomy aimed at one capability area rather than the whole labor market.

sections.heading: What makes a skills taxonomy usable?

blocks.text: A usable taxonomy is detailed enough to support its intended decisions and small enough to maintain. The World Economic Forum toolkit lists six properties to check, whichever taxonomy an organization adopts.

items: **Dynamic:** reflects a changing labor market and can be updated regularly.
**Comprehensive:** describes skills for all the roles or occupations in scope.
**Interoperable:** supports rather than conflicts with existing standards.
**Accessible:** uses plain language and a design people can use.
**Customizable:** can reflect the needs of the organization and its national context.
**Granular:** lets users explore specific skills and adjacencies at the level of detail they need.

blocks.text: Granularity is the hardest choice. A taxonomy with thousands of fine-grained skills supports precise matching and analytics but is costly to maintain and hard for managers to use in conversations. A taxonomy with a few hundred broader skills is easier to govern but may hide the specific capability a regulated task depends on. Many organizations keep a broad internal layer and map it to a granular public taxonomy for reporting.

sections.heading: How is a skills taxonomy different from a competency framework or a skills matrix?

blocks.text: A skills taxonomy is a vocabulary; a [competency framework](/glossary/competency-framework) is a standard; a [skills matrix](/glossary/skills-matrix) is a record. The taxonomy names and defines skills, the framework states what level of which skills each role needs and how that is evidenced, and the matrix shows which people currently meet it.

items: **Taxonomy vs competency framework:** the framework adds performance criteria and assessment evidence. See [competency framework vs skills framework](/compare/competency-framework-vs-skills-framework).

**Taxonomy vs ontology:** a taxonomy mainly arranges skills in a hierarchy; an ontology adds typed relationships such as "is essential for" or "requires". See [skills taxonomy vs skills ontology](/compare/skills-taxonomy-vs-skills-ontology).

**Taxonomy vs job task analysis:** a [job task analysis](/glossary/job-task-analysis) studies one job to find its tasks and the skills behind them; the taxonomy supplies consistent names for what the analysis finds.

blocks.text: Each entry would also carry an owner, a version and, where relevant, the matching concept in a public classification. That mapping is what lets internal data be compared with labor market data later.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry works one layer below the skills taxonomy: it models the concepts, obligations and assessment points that a skill depends on, and links them to the skill labels an organization already uses. The taxonomy stays the shared vocabulary, while the knowledge structure underneath shows what each skill actually requires and where it is checked.

faqs.q: Should an organization build its own skills taxonomy or adopt a public one?
faqs.a: Most organizations adopt a public taxonomy as the base and add internal skills where the public one is too general, such as skills tied to proprietary products or internal procedures. Keeping a mapping to the public source preserves interoperability with recruitment, labor market and qualification data.

faqs.q: How many skills should a taxonomy contain?
faqs.a: There is no correct number. Public classifications hold thousands of concepts because they cover whole economies. An internal taxonomy should hold enough skills to describe the work that matters to its decisions, at a granularity managers and assessors can actually use. If skills are never assigned to roles or assessed, the taxonomy is probably too fine.

faqs.q: Does a skills taxonomy need proficiency levels?
faqs.a: Not always. A taxonomy can work as a pure vocabulary. Proficiency levels become necessary when the taxonomy is used to set role requirements, measure gaps or assess people, because a skill name alone does not say how well someone must perform it.

faqs.q: How often should a skills taxonomy be updated?
faqs.a: Review it on a fixed cycle and whenever technology, regulation or role design changes the work. Public taxonomies publish versioned releases, so an internal taxonomy mapped to them should record which version each mapping refers to.
